1.1: - **LO 1.1.A** Explain how the properties of water resulting from polarity and hydrogen bonding affect its biological function. - EK 1.1.A.1 — Water's polarity (polar covalent H–O bonds) enables hydrogen bonding; high specific heat capacity maintains homeostatic temperature; high heat of vaporization enables evaporative cooling. - EK 1.1.A.2 — Hydrogen bonds between water molecules produce cohesion, adhesion, and surface tension.
1.2: - **LO 1.2.A** Describe the composition of macromolecules required by living organisms. - EK 1.2.A.1 — C, H, O are most prevalent in biological molecules; S builds proteins, P builds phospholipids/nucleic acids, N builds nucleic acids.
1.3: - **LO 1.3.A** Describe the chemical reactions that build and break biological macromolecules. - EK 1.3.A.1 — Hydrolysis cleaves a polymer bond by adding water (H to one monomer, OH to the other). - EK 1.3.A.2 — Dehydration synthesis joins two monomers via covalent bond, releasing water; repeated joining = polymerization.
1.4: - **LO 1.4.A** Describe the structure and function of carbohydrates. - EK 1.4.A.1 — Monosaccharides are monomers for polysaccharides (e.g. cellulose, starch, glycogen), joined by covalent bonds into linear or branched polymers. *Exclusion: specific carbohydrate polymer molecular structure is beyond exam scope.*
1.5: - **LO 1.5.A** Describe the structure and function of lipids. - EK 1.5.A.1 — Lipids are typically nonpolar/hydrophobic. Fatty acids: saturated = only single C–C bonds; unsaturated = ≥1 double bond causing kinks; more double bonds = more unsaturated = more liquid at room temp. - EK 1.5.A.2 — Functions: fats store energy/support function/insulate; steroids are hormones supporting growth, metabolism, homeostasis; cholesterol stabilizes animal membranes; phospholipids form the lipid bilayer. *Exclusion: specific lipid molecular structure beyond scope.*
1.6: - **LO 1.6.A** Describe the structure and function of DNA and RNA. - EK 1.6.A.1 — Nucleic acids encode information via nucleotide sequence; each nucleotide = 5-C sugar (deoxyribose/ribose) + phosphate + base (A, T, G, C, or U). - EK 1.6.A.2 — Linear sequence with 3'/5' ends; synthesis adds nucleotides to the 3' end. *Exclusion: specific nucleotide molecular structure beyond scope.* - EK 1.6.A.3 — DNA is an antiparallel double helix; A–T and C–G pair via H bonds in DNA; A–U in RNA. - EK 1.6.A.4 — DNA vs. RNA: deoxyribose vs. ribose; thymine vs. uracil; typically double- vs. single-stranded.
1.7: - **LO 1.7.A** Describe the structure and function of proteins. - EK 1.7.A.1 — Proteins are amino-acid chains joined by peptide bonds (carboxyl-to-amine). - EK 1.7.A.2 — Amino acid = central C + H + carboxyl + amine + variable R group (hydrophobic, hydrophilic, or ionic); R-group interactions drive local structure/function. - EK 1.7.A.3 — Amino acid sequence determines primary structure/overall shape. *Exclusion: specific amino acid molecular structure beyond scope.* - EK 1.7.A.4 — Secondary structure (alpha-helix, beta-sheet) from H-bonding between backbone atoms. - EK 1.7.A.5 — Tertiary structure (3D shape) from H-bonds, hydrophobic interactions, ionic interactions, disulfide bridges. - EK 1.7.A.6 — Quaternary structure from interactions between multiple polypeptides; all four levels determine function.
2.1: - **LO 2.1.A** Explain how the structure/function of subcellular components and organelles contribute to cell function. - EK 2.1.A.1 — Ribosomes (rRNA + protein) synthesize proteins per mRNA. - EK 2.1.A.2 — Endomembrane system (ER, Golgi, lysosomes, vacuoles, nuclear envelope, plasma membrane) modifies/packages/transports products. - EK 2.1.A.3 — ER: rough (ribosome-studded, protein synthesis) vs. smooth (detox, lipid synthesis). *Exclusion: specific smooth-ER functions in specialized cells beyond scope.* - EK 2.1.A.4 — Golgi: flattened sacs that fold/modify/package proteins for trafficking. *Exclusion: specific Golgi roles in lysosome/peroxisome/ secretory-vesicle enzyme synthesis beyond scope.* - EK 2.1.A.5 — Mitochondria: double membrane compartmentalizes aerobic respiration; convoluted inner membrane for efficient ATP synthesis. - EK 2.1.A.6 — Lysosomes: hydrolytic-enzyme sacs; digest material, drive apoptosis. - EK 2.1.A.7 — Vacuoles: large plant vacuole maintains turgor pressure; animal vacuoles smaller/more numerous, store materials. - EK 2.1.A.8 — Chloroplasts: double-membrane, site of photosynthesis. - *Source: CED V.1 (© 2025), printed pp. 49-51; confirmed by the Product Owner on 2026-10-01 as the latest edition.* - *Not in the CED (2026-10-01 check of printed pp. 49-51 and a full-text search):* *signal sequence / signal peptide, signal recognition particle (SRP), co-translational ER targeting, and sorting of proteins to specific organelles. The CED states only that rough ER has membrane-bound ribosomes and helps carry out protein synthesis (2.1.A.3.i), and that the endomembrane system works together to modify, package and transport proteins (2.1.A.2). Items must not depend on those mechanisms. The Golgi exclusion (2.1.A.4) also puts packaging of specific enzymes for lysosomes, peroxisomes and secretory vesicles out of scope.*
2.2: - **LO 2.2.A** Explain the effect of surface area-to-volume ratio on exchange between cells/organisms and environment. - EK 2.2.A.1 — SA:V affects nutrient/waste/thermal/chemical exchange (includes relevant volume/SA equations). - EK 2.2.A.2 — Smaller cells → higher SA:V → more efficient exchange; as volume grows SA:V drops, raising internal resource demand; membrane folds compensate; larger organisms have lower SA:V affecting heat exchange; smaller organisms generally have higher mass-specific metabolic rate.
2.3: - **LO 2.3.A** Describe the roles of each membrane component in maintaining internal environment. - EK 2.3.A.1 — Phospholipids: hydrophilic heads face out, hydrophobic tails face in. - EK 2.3.A.2 — Embedded proteins can be hydrophilic, hydrophobic, or both, oriented accordingly. - **LO 2.3.B** Describe the fluid mosaic model. - EK 2.3.B.1 — Membranes = phospholipid framework with mobile proteins, steroids (e.g. cholesterol), glycoproteins, glycolipids.
2.4: - **LO 2.4.A** Explain how membrane structure influences selective permeability. - EK 2.4.A.1 — Hydrophobic interior gives selective permeability. - EK 2.4.A.2 — Small nonpolar molecules (N₂, O₂, CO₂) cross freely; hydrophilic substances need channels/transport proteins. - EK 2.4.A.3 — Hydrocarbon tails block ions/polar molecules; small polar uncharged molecules (H₂O, NH₃) pass in small amounts. - **LO 2.4.B** Describe the role of the cell wall. - EK 2.4.B.1 — Cell walls (Bacteria, Archaea, Fungi, plants) provide structural boundary, permeability barrier, protection from osmotic lysis.
2.5: - **LO 2.5.A** Describe mechanisms for solute/water balance. - EK 2.5.A.1 — Selective permeability creates solute concentration gradients. - EK 2.5.A.2 — Passive transport: net high→low movement, no direct energy. - EK 2.5.A.3 — Active transport: requires energy, can move low→high. - **LO 2.5.B** Describe transport of large molecules across the membrane. - EK 2.5.B.1 — Endocytosis (membrane folds inward to engulf) / exocytosis (vesicle fuses with membrane to secrete) use energy.
2.6: - **LO 2.6.A** Explain how molecule structure affects membrane passage. - EK 2.6.A.1 — Charged ions (Na⁺, K⁺) need channel proteins; ion movement can polarize membranes. - EK 2.6.A.2 — Facilitated diffusion moves large polar molecules down gradient, no energy input. - EK 2.6.A.3 — Aquaporins transport large quantities of water.
2.7: - **LO 2.7.A** Explain how concentration gradients affect molecule movement. - EK 2.7.A.1 — Environments can be hypo-/hyper-/isotonic; water moves by osmosis high→low water potential (Ψ = Ψp + Ψs). - **LO 2.7.B** Explain how osmoregulation contributes to health/survival. - EK 2.7.B.1 — Growth/homeostasis maintained by constant cross-membrane movement. - EK 2.7.B.2 — Osmoregulation maintains water balance/solute composition; water moves low→high osmolarity (Ψs = −iCRT).
2.8: - **LO 2.8.A** Describe processes for ion/molecule movement across membranes. - EK 2.8.A.1 — Metabolic energy (e.g. ATP) required for active transport and electrochemical gradient maintenance; Na⁺/K⁺ pump and ATPase maintain membrane potential.
2.9: - **LO 2.9.A** Describe membrane-bound structures of the eukaryotic cell. - EK 2.9.A.1 — Membranes/membrane-bound organelles compartmentalize metabolic processes and enzymatic reactions. - **LO 2.9.B** Explain how internal membranes contribute to compartmentalized function. - EK 2.9.B.1 — Internal membranes minimize competing interactions and increase reaction surface area.
2.10: - **LO 2.10.A** Describe similarities/differences in compartmentalization between prokaryotes and eukaryotes. - EK 2.10.A.1 — Mitochondria/chloroplasts evolved from free-living prokaryotes via endosymbiosis. - EK 2.10.A.2 — Prokaryotes typically lack membrane-bound organelles but have specialized internal regions. - EK 2.10.A.3 — Eukaryotic internal membranes partition specialized regions.
3.1: - **LO 3.1.A** Explain how enzymes affect reaction rate. - EK 3.1.A.1 — Enzymes are protein catalysts that lower activation energy. - EK 3.1.A.2 — Enzyme-substrate complex model: substrate shape/charge must fit the active site.
3.2: - **LO 3.2.A** Explain how enzyme structure changes affect function. - EK 3.2.A.1 — Denaturation (temp/pH/chemical) eliminates catalytic ability; temp/pH outside optimum alters H-bonding and efficiency. - EK 3.2.A.2 — Denaturation is sometimes reversible. - **LO 3.2.B** Explain how cellular environment affects enzyme activity. - EK 3.2.B.1 — Relative substrate/product concentration affects reaction efficiency. - EK 3.2.B.2 — Higher temperature raises collision frequency/rate up to the optimum. - EK 3.2.B.3 — Competitive inhibitors bind the active site reversibly; noncompetitive inhibitors bind allosteric sites.
3.3: - **LO 3.3.A** Describe the role of energy in living organisms. - EK 3.3.A.1 — All living systems require energy input. - EK 3.3.A.2 — Ordered systems are consistent with the 1st/2nd laws of thermodynamics; energy input must exceed loss. *Exclusion: Gibbs free energy equation not required.* - EK 3.3.A.3 — Metabolic pathways are sequential; a product is typically the next step's reactant. - **LO 3.3.B** Explain how conserved processes support common ancestry. - EK 3.3.B.1 — Core pathways (glycolysis, oxidative phosphorylation) are conserved across Archaea, Bacteria, Eukarya.
3.4: enzyme names beyond ATP synthase are out of scope.)* - **LO 3.4.A** Describe photosynthetic processes and chloroplast structure. - EK 3.4.A.1 — Photosynthesis uses CO₂ + H₂O + light → carbohydrates + O₂; first evolved in prokaryotes; cyanobacterial photosynthesis produced Earth's oxygenated atmosphere. - EK 3.4.A.2 — Stroma (Calvin cycle site) and thylakoids (grana; light reactions, two photosystems + ETC). - EK 3.4.A.3 — Light reactions yield ATP and NADPH powering the Calvin cycle. - **LO 3.4.B** Explain how cells capture and transfer light energy. - EK 3.4.B.1 — ETC reactions occur in chloroplasts/mitochondria/prokaryotic membranes; electrons cross the thylakoid membrane, reducing NADP⁺ at photosystem I. *Exclusion: specific electron-carrier names/intermediates out of scope.* - EK 3.4.B.2 — Chlorophylls absorb light, boosting electrons in photosystems I/II; water splits to replace electrons lost at PS II. - EK 3.4.B.3 — PS I and II connected via ETC in the thylakoid membrane. - EK 3.4.B.4 — ETC establishes a proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane. - EK 3.4.B.5 — Chemiosmosis through ATP synthase drives photophosphorylation. - EK 3.4.B.6 — ATP/NADPH power Calvin-cycle carbohydrate production.
3.5: - **LO 3.5.A** Describe processes/structures allowing energy use from macromolecules. *Exclusion: specific electron carrier names, intermediates/ enzyme names out of scope.* - EK 3.5.A.1 — Respiration/fermentation synthesize ATP from macromolecules; occur in all life forms. - EK 3.5.A.2 — Aerobic respiration involves coordinated enzyme-catalyzed reactions. - EK 3.5.A.3 — ETC electron transfer builds a proton gradient (across inner mitochondrial membrane in eukaryotes, plasma membrane in prokaryotes); NADH/FADH₂ deliver electrons ending in O₂ (aerobic) or other acceptors (anaerobic); chemiosmosis through ATP synthase drives oxidative phosphorylation; decoupling generates heat for endotherm thermoregulation. - **LO 3.5.B** Explain how cells obtain energy from macromolecules. *(Exclusion: memorization of glycolysis/Krebs steps, structures, enzyme names out of scope.)* - EK 3.5.B.1 — Glycolysis: glucose → ATP, NADH, pyruvate. - EK 3.5.B.2 — Pyruvate → mitochondrion; Krebs cycle reduces NAD⁺/FAD, releases CO₂. - EK 3.5.B.3 — Krebs cycle occurs in the matrix. - EK 3.5.B.4 — NADH/FADH₂ carry electrons from glycolysis/Krebs to the ETC. - EK 3.5.B.5 — ETC builds the proton gradient (matrix pH higher than intermembrane space). - EK 3.5.B.6 — Fermentation lets glycolysis proceed without O₂, producing alcohol or lactic acid.
4.1: - **LO 4.1.A** Describe ways cells communicate. - EK 4.1.A.1 — Direct contact or chemical signaling at a distance. - **LO 4.1.B** Explain short- vs. long-distance cell communication. - EK 4.1.B.1 — Short-distance: local regulators act on nearby cells. - EK 4.1.B.2 — Signals can travel long distances to other cell types.
4.2: - **LO 4.2.A** Describe components of a signal transduction pathway. - EK 4.2.A.1 — Pathways link signal reception to cellular response. - EK 4.2.A.2 — Many pathways involve protein modification/phosphorylation cascades. - **LO 4.2.B** Describe how pathway components produce a cellular response. - EK 4.2.B.1 — Ligand recognized by a receptor (ligand-binding domain specificity; GPCRs as eukaryotic example; surface/cytoplasm/nuclear receptors). - EK 4.2.B.2 — Cascades relay/amplify signal (shape change, second messengers like cAMP, hormones via bloodstream, ligand-gated channels).
4.3: - **LO 4.3.A** Describe cellular responses elicited by a pathway. - EK 4.3.A.1 — Signal transduction can change gene expression/function, alter phenotype, or trigger apoptosis. - **LO 4.3.B** Explain how signaling-molecule structure changes affect pathway activity. - EK 4.3.B.1 — Changes to pathway molecules alter downstream transduction. - EK 4.3.B.2 — Chemicals interacting with any component may activate/inhibit the pathway.
4.4: - **LO 4.4.A** Explain how feedback maintains homeostasis. - EK 4.4.A.1 — Negative feedback reduces the stimulus toward set point; positive feedback amplifies it until system change occurs.
4.5: - **LO 4.5.A** Describe events of the cell cycle. - EK 4.5.A.1 — Interphase (G1: organelle/cytosolic duplication; S: DNA replicates into sister chromatids; G2: protein synthesis, ATP production, centrosome replication), mitosis, cytokinesis; G0 = non-dividing state; checkpoints can hold the cycle. - **LO 4.5.B** Explain how mitosis transmits chromosomes to daughter cells. - EK 4.5.B.1 — Prophase (condensation, spindle forms) → Metaphase (align at equator) → Anaphase (sister chromatids separate) → Telophase (envelope reforms) → Cytokinesis (cleavage furrow / cell plate).
4.6: - **LO 4.6.A** Describe checkpoints regulating the cell cycle. - EK 4.6.A.1 — Internal controls/checkpoints regulate progression. - EK 4.6.A.2 — Cyclin–CDK interactions control the cycle. *Exclusion: specific cyclin-CDK pairs/growth factors beyond scope.* - **LO 4.6.B** Describe effects of cell-cycle disruption. - EK 4.6.B.1 — Disruptions can cause cancer or apoptosis.
5.1: - **LO 5.1.A** Explain how meiosis transmits chromosomes across generations. - EK 5.1.A.1 — Meiosis produces haploid gametes from diploid organisms. - EK 5.1.A.2 — Meiosis I: Prophase I (synapsis, chiasmata) → Metaphase I (homolog pairs align) → Anaphase I (homologs separate) → Telophase I (two haploid cells). - EK 5.1.A.3 — Meiosis II: Prophase II → Metaphase II → Anaphase II (sister chromatids separate) → Telophase II (four haploid cells). - **LO 5.1.B** Describe similarities/differences between mitosis and meiosis. - EK 5.1.B.1 — Both use a spindle apparatus but differ in cell count and genetic content of products.
5.2: - **LO 5.2.A** Explain how meiosis generates genetic diversity. - EK 5.2.A.1 — Correct homolog/sister-chromatid separation gives each gamete a proper haploid mixed set; nondisjunction disrupts this. - EK 5.2.A.2 — Crossing over in prophase I increases diversity. - EK 5.2.A.3 — Sexual reproduction increases variation via crossing over, random assortment, fertilization. *Exclusion: species-specific reproduction-cycle details out of scope.*
5.3: - **LO 5.3.A** Explain inheritance per Mendel's laws. - EK 5.3.A.1 — Segregation and independent assortment apply to genes on different chromosomes. - EK 5.3.A.2 — Fertilization restores diploidy, increases variation: probability rules apply to single-gene inheritance; monohybrid/dihybrid/ test crosses determine dominance; genotype = inherited alleles; phenotype = observable expression; autosomal/linked/sex-linked patterns predictable from pedigrees; Punnett squares predict outcomes. *Equations:* P(A or B) = P(A)+P(B) if mutually exclusive; P(A and B) = P(A)×P(B) if independent.
5.4: - **LO 5.4.A** Explain deviations from Mendel's model. - EK 5.4.A.1 — Genetic linkage (linked genes co-segregate; map distance via recombination frequency); codominance (both alleles expressed); incomplete dominance (blended phenotype). - EK 5.4.A.2 — Sex-linked traits determined by sex-chromosome genes, predictable from pedigrees (illustrative: ZW in birds, haplodiploidy in bees). - EK 5.4.A.3 — Pleiotropy: one gene affects multiple traits that don't segregate independently. - EK 5.4.A.4 — Non-nuclear inheritance: organelle DNA randomly assorts; animal mitochondrial traits typically maternal (via egg); plant organelle traits typically maternal (via ovule, not pollen).
5.5: - **LO 5.5.A** Explain how one genotype yields multiple phenotypes across environments. - EK 5.5.A.1 — Environment influences gene expression → phenotypic plasticity (illustrative: human height/weight, soil-pH flower color, seasonal fur color, temperature-dependent sex determination, UV-induced melanin, yeast mating-type pheromones).
6.1: - **LO 6.1.A** Describe structures passing hereditary information. - EK 6.1.A.1 — Prokaryotes: circular chromosome; eukaryotes: multiple linear histone-condensed chromosomes. - EK 6.1.A.2 — Both can contain plasmids. - **LO 6.1.B** Describe characteristics making DNA hereditary material. - EK 6.1.B.1 — Conserved base pairing: purines (A, G) pair with pyrimidines (C, T, U).
6.2: - **LO 6.2.A** Describe mechanisms copying genetic information. - EK 6.2.A.1 — Semiconservative, 5'→3' synthesis; helicase unwinds; topoisomerase relaxes supercoiling; DNA pol needs RNA primers; leading strand continuous, lagging discontinuous; ligase joins fragments. *Exclusion: enzymes/steps beyond helicase, topoisomerase, DNA pol, ligase, RNA pol out of scope.*
6.3: - **LO 6.3.A** Describe DNA→RNA→protein information flow. - EK 6.3.A.1 — mRNA carries info to ribosome; tRNA binds amino acids via anticodon-codon pairing; rRNA is a functional ribosome component. - EK 6.3.A.2 — RNA polymerase uses a single DNA template strand. - EK 6.3.A.3 — mRNA synthesized 5'→3', template read 3'→5'. - EK 6.3.A.4 — Eukaryotic mRNA modified post-transcriptionally: poly-A tail, GTP cap, intron excision/exon splicing (incl. alternative splicing).
6.4: - **LO 6.4.A** Explain how genotype determines phenotype. - EK 6.4.A.1 — Translation occurs on ribosomes (cytoplasm; rough ER surface in eukaryotes). - EK 6.4.A.2 — In prokaryotes, translation is co-transcriptional. - EK 6.4.A.3 — Initiation (AUG/methionine) → elongation (triplet codons, redundant/near-universal code as common-ancestry evidence, tRNA delivery) → termination (stop codon). *Exclusion: factor details beyond scope; genetic-code memorization beyond start codon out of scope.* - EK 6.4.A.4 — Retroviruses: reverse transcriptase makes DNA from RNA, integrates into host genome.
6.5: - **LO 6.5.A** Describe interactions regulating gene expression. - EK 6.5.A.1 — Regulatory DNA sequences interact with regulatory proteins; genes may be constitutive or inducible. - EK 6.5.A.2 — Epigenetic (reversible DNA/histone) changes affect expression. - EK 6.5.A.3 — Phenotype depends on gene combination/expression level: differentiation from tissue-specific expression; transcription-factor induction drives developmental gene sequences. - **LO 6.5.B** Explain how regulatory-sequence location relates to function. - EK 6.5.B.1 — Prokaryotes: inducible/repressible operons; eukaryotes: shared transcription factors across gene groups.
6.6: - **LO 6.6.A** Explain how transcription-factor binding affects expression and phenotype. - EK 6.6.A.1 — RNA pol/transcription factors bind promoter/enhancer sequences to initiate transcription. - EK 6.6.A.2 — Negative regulators inhibit expression by blocking transcription. - **LO 6.6.B** Explain the link between gene-expression regulation and phenotypic differences. - EK 6.6.B.1 — Regulation produces differential expression, affecting cell products/functions. - EK 6.6.B.2 — Certain small RNAs regulate gene expression.
6.7: - **LO 6.7.A** Describe types of mutation. - EK 6.7.A.1 — Point (substitution), frameshift (insertion/deletion), nonsense (premature stop), silent (no amino-acid effect). *Exclusion: specific mutation knowledge beyond scope.* - **LO 6.7.B** Explain how genotype changes cause phenotype changes. - EK 6.7.B.1 — Replication/repair errors + external factors (radiation, reactive chemicals) cause mutations, a source of variation. - EK 6.7.B.2 — Mitosis/meiosis errors: nondisjunction → aneuploidy; chromosome-number/structure changes → developmental/genetic disorders. *Exclusion: specific disorder knowledge beyond scope.* - **LO 6.7.C** Explain how DNA-sequence changes feed natural selection. - EK 6.7.C.1 — Horizontal gene transfer (transformation, transduction, conjugation, transposition) and viral recombination increase variation; these processes are evolutionarily conserved.
6.8: - **LO 6.8.A** Explain genetic-engineering techniques for analyzing/ manipulating DNA. - EK 6.8.A.1 — Gel electrophoresis (size/charge separation); PCR (denature/anneal/extend amplification); bacterial transformation; DNA sequencing → fingerprint comparison. *Exclusion: technique-detail knowledge beyond scope.*
7.1: - **LO 7.1.A** Describe the causes of natural selection. - EK 7.1.A.1 — Natural selection is a major mechanism of evolution. - EK 7.1.A.2 — Competition for limited resources causes differential survival/reproduction of favorable phenotypes. - **LO 7.1.B** Explain how natural selection affects populations. - EK 7.1.B.1 — Fitness is measured by reproductive success. - EK 7.1.B.2 — Fluctuating environments affect rate/direction of evolution.
7.2: - **LO 7.2.A** Describe the importance of phenotypic variation. - EK 7.2.A.1 — Selection acts on phenotypic variation. - EK 7.2.A.2 — Environments change and apply selective pressure. - EK 7.2.A.3 — Phenotypic variation can raise or lower fitness by environment. - **LO 7.2.B** Explain how molecular variation connects to fitness. - EK 7.2.B.1 — Variation in cellular molecule number/type affects survival/reproduction across environments.
7.3: - **LO 7.3.A** Explain how humans affect population diversity. - EK 7.3.A.1 — Artificial selection lets humans affect variation in other species.
7.4: - **LO 7.4.A** Explain how random occurrences affect a population's genetic makeup. - EK 7.4.A.1 — Mutation adds variation; genetic drift = nonselective allele-frequency change in small populations; bottleneck effect; founder effect; migration causes gene flow. - **LO 7.4.B** Describe the role of random processes in population evolution. - EK 7.4.B.1 — Mutations create variation; drift lets small populations diverge; gene flow prevents divergence into separate species. - **LO 7.4.C** Describe change in population genetic makeup over time. - EK 7.4.C.1 — Allele-frequency change is evidence of evolution.
7.5: - **LO 7.5.A** Describe conditions under which allele/genotype frequencies change. - EK 7.5.A.1 — HWE requires large population, no migration, no new mutations, random mating, no selection — a null hypothesis, never fully met. - EK 7.5.A.2 — Allele frequencies computed from genotype frequencies (p²+2pq+q²=1, p+q=1).
7.6: - **LO 7.6.A** Describe types of evidence for evolution. - EK 7.6.A.1 — Geographical, geological, physical, biochemical, mathematical evidence. - **LO 7.6.B** Explain how morphological/biochemical/geological data show change over time. - EK 7.6.B.1 — Fossil dating (rock age, isotope decay); morphological homologies incl. vestigial structures indicate common ancestry. - EK 7.6.B.2 — DNA/protein sequence comparison provides evidence for common ancestry.
7.7: - **LO 7.7.A** Describe cellular/molecular evidence for eukaryotic common ancestry. - EK 7.7.A.1 — Membrane-bound organelles, linear chromosomes, intron- containing genes.
7.8: - **LO 7.8.A** Explain evolution as an ongoing process. - EK 7.8.A.1 — Genomic change over time, fossil-record change, antibiotic/ pesticide/herbicide/chemotherapy resistance, emergent pathogen disease.
7.9: - **LO 7.9.A** Describe evidence used to infer evolutionary relationships. - EK 7.9.A.1 — Trees/cladograms show testable evolutionary relationships. - EK 7.9.A.2 — Trees show time (calibrated by fossils/molecular clock); cladograms do not. - EK 7.9.A.3 — Traits gained/lost build trees; shared derived characters indicate common ancestry; molecular data typically more reliable than morphological. - **LO 7.9.B** Explain how trees/cladograms infer relatedness. - EK 7.9.B.1 — Nodes = most recent common ancestor. - EK 7.9.B.2 — Built from morphological and molecular-sequence similarity. - EK 7.9.B.3 — Trees are hypotheses, constantly revised.
7.10: - **LO 7.10.A** Describe conditions under which new species arise. - EK 7.10.A.1 — Speciation = reproductive isolation of two populations. - EK 7.10.A.2 — Biological species concept: interbreeding group producing viable, fertile offspring. - **LO 7.10.B** Describe rate of speciation under different conditions. - EK 7.10.B.1 — Punctuated equilibrium (rapid change after stasis) vs. gradualism (slow, continuous). - EK 7.10.B.2 — Divergent evolution from habitat adaptation; adaptive radiation speeds speciation. - EK 7.10.B.3 — Convergent evolution from similar selective pressures on different lineages. - **LO 7.10.C** Explain mechanisms driving speciation. - EK 7.10.C.1 — Sympatric (geographic overlap) vs. allopatric (isolation) speciation. - EK 7.10.C.2 — Pre- and post-zygotic isolating mechanisms prevent gene flow.
7.11: - **LO 7.11.A** Explain how genetic diversity affects environmental resilience. - EK 7.11.A.1 — Low diversity risks decline/extinction; higher diversity is more resilient; alleles adaptive in one condition can be deleterious in another.
7.12: - **LO 7.12.A** Describe evidence for origin-of-life models. - EK 7.12.A.1 — Earth formed ~4.6 bya; hostile until ~3.9 bya; earliest fossil life ~3.5 bya. - EK 7.12.A.2 — RNA world hypothesis: RNA replication ensured genetic continuity; base-pairing enabled replication; genetically encoded proteins were not yet involved as catalysts.
8.1: - **LO 8.1.A** Explain behavioral/physiological response to environmental change. - EK 8.1.A.1 — Organisms respond via behavioral and physiological mechanisms. *Exclusion: specific mechanisms beyond scope.* - EK 8.1.A.2 — Organisms exchange information, altering behavior in response to internal/external cues. - **LO 8.1.B** Explain how behavioral responses affect fitness/population success. - EK 8.1.B.1 — Visual, audible, tactile, electrical, chemical signals indicate dominance, food, territory, reproductive success. *Exclusion: specific mechanisms beyond scope.* - EK 8.1.B.2 — Communication response is vital to selection/evolution; innate/learned behavior and cooperation raise fitness.
8.2: - **LO 8.2.A** Describe strategies for acquiring/using energy. - EK 8.2.A.1 — Endotherms/ectotherms regulate temperature differently; net energy gain → growth/reproduction, net loss → decline/death. - EK 8.2.A.2 — Reproductive strategy (sexual vs. asexual) varies with energy availability. - **LO 8.2.B** Explain how energy flows and matter cycles through trophic levels. - EK 8.2.B.1 — Organization: populations, communities, ecosystems, biomes. - EK 8.2.B.2 — Energy flows one-way; matter cycles via biogeochemical cycles. - EK 8.2.B.3 — Biogeochemical cycles include abiotic/biotic reservoirs and cycling processes. - EK 8.2.B.4 — Hydrologic cycle: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, transpiration. - EK 8.2.B.5 — Carbon cycle: photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, combustion. - EK 8.2.B.6 — Nitrogen cycle: fixation, assimilation, ammonification, nitrification, denitrification (largely microbial). - EK 8.2.B.7 — Phosphorus cycle: weathering → soil/water → producers → consumers → decomposition/excretion. - **LO 8.2.C** Explain how energy-availability changes affect populations/ communities/ecosystems. - EK 8.2.C.1 — Energy availability affects population size. - EK 8.2.C.2 — Energy changes disrupt trophic-level size/number (producers, primary–quaternary consumers, decomposers); producer biomass changes ripple upward. - **LO 8.2.D** Explain how autotrophs/heterotrophs enable energy flow. - EK 8.2.D.1 — Autotrophs: photosynthesis or chemosynthesis (anaerobic). - EK 8.2.D.2 — Heterotrophs (carnivores, herbivores, omnivores, decomposers, scavengers) metabolize consumed organic matter.
8.3: - **LO 8.3.A** Describe factors influencing population growth dynamics. - EK 8.3.A.1 — Populations = same-species individuals interacting with each other/environment. - EK 8.3.A.2 — Growth depends on birth/death rate and size (dN/dt = B−D); unconstrained reproduction → exponential growth (dN/dt = r_max·N).
8.4: - **LO 8.4.A** Explain how density affects/is determined by resource availability. - EK 8.4.A.1 — Carrying capacity (K) = sustainable abundance given resources. - EK 8.4.A.2 — Density-dependent/independent limits produce logistic growth (dN/dt = r_max·N·[(K−N)/K]).
8.5: - **LO 8.5.A** Describe community structure via composition/diversity. - EK 8.5.A.1 — Measured via species composition and diversity (Simpson's Diversity Index). - **LO 8.5.B** Explain how population interactions shape community structure. - EK 8.5.B.1 — Communities = interacting populations, changing over time. - EK 8.5.B.2 — Interactions determine access to energy/matter. - EK 8.5.B.3 — Positive/negative relationships modeled via predator/prey, cooperation, trophic cascades, niche partitioning. - EK 8.5.B.4 — Competition, predation, symbioses (parasitism, mutualism, commensalism) drive population dynamics.
8.6: - **LO 8.6.A** Describe the relationship between ecosystem diversity and resilience. - EK 8.6.A.1 — Less diverse ecosystems are less resilient to change. - EK 8.6.A.2 — Keystone species, producers, essential abiotic/biotic factors maintain diversity. - **LO 8.6.B** Explain how adding/removing a component affects ecosystem structure. - EK 8.6.B.1 — Keystone-species effects are disproportionate to abundance; removal often causes collapse.
8.7: - **LO 8.7.A** (Big Idea 1) Explain interaction between environment and preexisting variation. - EK 8.7.A.1 — Adaptation = genetic variation favored by selection. - EK 8.7.A.2 — Heterozygote advantage: heterozygote fitness exceeds either homozygote. - EK 8.7.A.3 — Mutations are not directed by environmental pressure. - **LO 8.7.B** (Big Idea 4) Explain how invasive species affect ecosystem dynamics. - EK 8.7.B.1 — Invasive species exploit niches free of predators/ competitors or outcompete natives. - **LO 8.7.C** (Big Idea 4) Describe human activities that change ecosystem structure. - EK 8.7.C.1 — Human impact accelerates extinctions, incl. biomagnification and eutrophication. - **LO 8.7.D** (Big Idea 4) Explain how geological/meteorological activity changes ecosystems. - EK 8.7.D.1 — Such events affect habitat and ecosystem distribution (illustrated by biogeographical studies).
